questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl of normal weight has bilateral painless swelling at the angles of the jaw, eroded dental enamel and calluses over the dorsum of the hand. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Parotid hypertrophy, enamel erosion and Russell sign (knuckle calluses from inducing vomiting) indicate bulimia; weight is usually normal. Restrictive anorexia shows low weight, lanugo and bradycardia.
questions.note: BN: parotid hypertrophy, enamel erosion, Russell sign (knuckle calluses).

questions.stem: In the patient with recurrent self-induced vomiting, which blood result pattern is expected?
questions.explain: Vomiting loses HCl; volume depletion triggers aldosterone, wasting K⁺ and H⁺ → hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Laxative abuse instead tends to give a normal anion-gap (hyperchloraemic) acidosis.
questions.note: BN: hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old with anorexia nervosa is seen in clinic. Which finding is an indication for hospital admission according to the criteria in your notes?
questions.explain: Admit AN with HR under 40, SBP under 80, temperature under 35.5 °C, %mBMI under 70%, or syncope. The other values are above these thresholds (though many guidelines, e.g. SAHM, admit at less extreme values such as HR <50).
questions.note: Admit AN: HR under 40, SBP under 80, temp under 35.5 °C, %mBMI under 70%, syncope.

questions.stem: A severely malnourished 14-year-old with anorexia is admitted and started on nasogastric feeding. On day 3 she develops weakness, confusion and heart failure. Which electrolyte abnormality is the key cause?
questions.explain: Refeeding syndrome: insulin surge drives phosphate (with K⁺ and Mg²⁺) into cells; hypophosphataemia depletes ATP and 2,3-DPG → weakness, confusion, heart failure. Potassium falls rather than rises.
questions.note: Refeeding: key electrolyte disturbance hypophosphataemia.

questions.stem: What is the first-line treatment for a 14-year-old with anorexia nervosa who is medically stable for outpatient care?
questions.explain: Family-based therapy (Maudsley) is first-line for adolescent AN. SSRIs (fluoxetine) plus psychotherapy are used in bulimia; medication has little role in AN weight restoration.
questions.note: Family-based therapy first-line for adolescent AN; bulimia: psychotherapy ± SSRIs (fluoxetine).

questions.stem: An 8-year-old has had periumbilical pain most school-day mornings for 4 months, never at weekends or holidays. Growth, examination and screening bloods are normal; the pain started after her parents separated. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Explain brain-gut link, avoid more tests, see one doctor regularly
Upper GI endoscopy and colonoscopy to exclude IBD
Abdominal CT to exclude malrotation and intussusception
Refer to paediatric surgery for a diagnostic laparoscopy
questions.explain: This is functional abdominal pain (commonest psychosomatic complaint), linked to stress and possibly separation anxiety/school avoidance. Without red flags, avoid endless tests; regular visits with a single physician, address stressors and screen for self-harm.
questions.note: Somatic symptoms: monthly visits with a single physician; screen self-harm.

cards.front: Compare the clinical signs of anorexia and bulimia nervosa.
cards.back: AN: low weight, bradycardia, hypotension, lanugo, amenorrhoea (low GnRH), mitral valve prolapse. BN: normal weight, parotid hypertrophy, enamel erosion, Russell sign, hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.

cards.front: What are the admission criteria for anorexia nervosa (per your notes)?
cards.back: HR under 40 • SBP under 80 • temperature under 35.5 °C • %mBMI under 70% • syncope. On refeeding watch hypophosphataemia (refeeding syndrome).

cards.front: How do you manage psychosomatic (functional) symptoms in children?
cards.back: Exclude red flags but avoid endless tests • explain stress → HPA/brain-gut axis → visceral hypersensitivity • address school, bullying, family conflict, abuse • monthly visits with one physician • screen for self-harm.
